title: Scientists Detect Alien Radio Signals From Distant Exoplanet, BBC Sky at Night Reports
body:
Astronomers have for the first time isolated a steady radio signal that can be traced to a single exoplanet, rather than to the broader star‑planet system that usually produces such emissions. The breakthrough, achieved with South Africa’s MeerKAT radio‑telescope array, offers a new window onto the magnetic environments of worlds beyond the Solar System and could eventually help scientists assess their habitability.

The detection was made while monitoring the ultra‑cool dwarf star GJ 1151, located about 30 light‑years from Earth in the constellation Ursa Major. Earlier observations had revealed a faint, broadband radio glow that could have originated from either the star or an orbiting companion. By employing MeerKAT’s high‑resolution imaging and a series of targeted follow‑up scans, the research team was able to pinpoint the source of the emission to a planet roughly the size of Earth that orbits the star every 2.5 days. The planet, designated GJ 1151 b, appears to generate a magnetic field strong enough to accelerate charged particles and produce the observed radio waves.

Radio emissions are a hallmark of magnetic activity. In our own Solar System, Jupiter’s powerful magnetosphere creates intense decametric radiation that can be detected from Earth. Until now, the only confirmed exoplanetary radio signatures have been indirect, inferred from the interaction between a star’s wind and a planet’s magnetosphere or from flares that could be linked to planetary influence. The new measurement marks the first instance where the signal’s spatial origin aligns directly with a planetary body, confirming that exoplanets can be radio beacons in their own right.

The discovery carries significant implications for exoplanet science. Magnetic fields act as protective shields, deflecting harmful stellar wind particles and preserving atmospheres over geological timescales. By measuring the strength and structure of a planet’s magnetosphere through its radio output, researchers can infer how well the world might retain an atmosphere—an essential factor in assessing its potential to host life. Moreover, the technique opens a path to studying planets that are otherwise invisible to optical or infrared telescopes, especially those orbiting active, low‑mass stars where traditional detection methods struggle.

The team’s analysis suggests that GJ 1151 b’s magnetic field may be comparable to Earth’s, despite the planet’s close‑in orbit that subjects it to intense stellar radiation. This raises intriguing questions about how such a field could be generated and sustained under extreme conditions. Some theorists propose that tidal heating and rapid rotation could drive a dynamo effect stronger than previously thought. Others caution that the observed radio power might be amplified by interactions with the star’s wind, meaning the planet’s intrinsic field could be weaker. Ongoing observations with MeerKAT and the upcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will aim to resolve these ambiguities by mapping the emission’s variability over time.

Looking ahead, the ability to directly detect exoplanetary radio signals could transform the hunt for Earth‑like worlds. As radio telescopes become more sensitive, astronomers anticipate cataloguing magnetic signatures from dozens, perhaps hundreds, of nearby planets. Such a census would complement existing surveys that measure mass, radius and atmospheric composition, offering a more complete picture of planetary environments. If magnetic fields prove to be a reliable proxy for atmospheric retention, future missions could prioritize radio‑active planets in the search for biosignatures. The breakthrough with GJ 1151 b thus not only confirms a long‑standing prediction about exoplanet magnetism but also charts a promising course for the next generation of planetary exploration.
